clue.text: Second Australian retired, creating buzz

indicators.note: retired means withdrawn or gone back, so the two pieces are read in reverse order

parts.note: a mo is a moment or second
Oz is slang for Australia, so Australian gives OZ

explanation.surface: An Australian second, having retired from tennis, gets everyone talking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'retired' turns MOOZ round into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To zoom is to move fast with a humming sound, a synonym of buzz along.

clue.text: See 23
Ball primarily hacked and cut thus?

definitions.text: Ball primarily hacked and cut thus?

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so only the first letter of ball is taken
cut means chopped about, so the letters of the next two words are rearranged

explanation.surface: A tennis shot where the ball is sliced with a reverse swing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cut' rearranges HACKEDAND into ACKHANDED after the B; read whole, the clue describes such a shot, so it is an all-in-one.
explanation.definitionFit: A backhanded stroke is played with the back of the hand facing forward, often sliced or cut.

clue.text: Common resident put millions into joint set-up

indicators.note: into says the abbreviation goes inside the other piece
in a down clue set up means turned upward, so the joint is read from bottom to top

parts.note: the elbow is a joint of the arm
M is the abbreviation for million(s)

explanation.surface: Someone local invests millions in a shared business venture.
explanation.walkthrough: 'set-up' turns ELBOW into WOBLE, and M goes 'into' it. The Wombles are furry fictional creatures from a British children's series who live on Wimbledon Common.
explanation.definitionFit: The Wombles live on Wimbledon Common in the British children's books and TV show, so one is a resident there.

clue.text: Old warrior caused upset with Roger losing heart

indicators.note: upset means knocked over, so the letters of caused and the remaining Roger letters are rearranged
losing heart means the middle of Roger is dropped, keeping just its first and last letters

explanation.surface: An ancient fighter brought about Roger's defeat after he lost his nerve.
explanation.walkthrough: 'losing heart' leaves RR from Roger, and 'upset' shuffles CAUSED with RR.
explanation.definitionFit: Crusaders were medieval soldiers who fought in the Holy Land, a kind of warrior of old.

clue.text: Top Russian's rackets are mostly confiscated

indicators.note: most of the words rackets are is taken away, leaving only a short run of their letters across the word break

explanation.surface: A Russian tennis star has most of her rackets impounded.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mostly confiscated' leaves a short run straddling rackeTS ARe.
explanation.definitionFit: The tsar was the emperor and supreme ruler of Russia before 1917.

clue.text: Eg Ivanisevich or Seles in jail with huge loo?

parts.note: OS stands for outsize, very large
lav, short for lavatory, is another word for loo

explanation.surface: Two Balkan tennis players imagined locked up in a prison with a giant toilet.
explanation.walkthrough: Goran Ivanisevic and Monica Seles were both born in the former Yugoslavia, here in an older spelling with J.
explanation.definitionFit: Both players came from the former Yugoslavia, so each is an example of a Yugoslav national.

clue.text: The chances of first finding big cups for ladies

indicators.note: first means just the opening letter of the word of is taken

parts.note: DD is a large bra cup size, so plural DDs

explanation.surface: Wondering about the likelihood of first spotting large trophies for women.
explanation.walkthrough: 'big cups for ladies' looks like trophies in the women's event, but DD is a bra size.
explanation.definitionFit: Odds are the probabilities or likelihoods quoted in betting, the same as chances.

clue.text: Met fan in old gym — amateur working out with Roger

parts.note: PE is physical education, school gym

indicators.note: working out means exercising, here also solving, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A New York Metropolitan Opera fan exercises in a gym with Roger Federer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Met' is not a past tense but New York's Metropolitan Opera; 'working out' fits the gym surface while signalling the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: The Met is the Metropolitan Opera House, so a fan of it is one who regularly attends opera.

clue.text: Two 14 back to lead group of players

indicators.note: back to lead says the final letter goes to the front

parts.note: two doubles, with 14 standing for doubles, makes four times, quads

explanation.surface: A team where two doubles pairings rotate positions to the net.
explanation.walkthrough: 14 is DOUBLES; two of them make QUADS, and 'back to lead' moves the last S to the front.
explanation.definitionFit: A squad is a team or set of players from which a side is picked.

clue.text: Maria's debut in Slovakia capital

indicators.note: debut means a first appearance, so only Maria's first letter is taken

parts.note: SK is the international code for Slovakia

explanation.surface: Maria Sharapova makes her first appearance in a tournament in Slovakia.
explanation.walkthrough: Minsk is the capital of Belarus, not Slovakia, despite the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Minsk is the capital city of Belarus.

clue.text: See 29
Lose cool in good old fight against Edberg at the start

parts.note: to spar is to fight or box

indicators.note: at the start means just the first letter of Edberg

explanation.surface: Losing one's temper in a vintage match against Stefan Edberg early on.
explanation.walkthrough: GO SPARE is British slang for becoming furious.
explanation.definitionFit: Going spare is British slang for becoming very angry, so losing one's temper.

clue.text: In which, at the outset, gritty Andy Murray expects success

definitions.text: In which, at the outset, gritty Andy Murray expects success

indicators.note: at the outset means the first letter of each following word is used

explanation.surface: A determined Andy Murray anticipates winning these.
explanation.walkthrough: The initials of the last five words spell the answer, and the whole clue describes where a player hopes to win.
explanation.definitionFit: In tennis a set is won by taking games, so they are where a player wants success.

clue.text: See 17
Regular lawn manicure ordered, contrary to US conventions

indicators.note: ordered means put in a new arrangement, so the letters are rearranged
regular means every other letter of lawn is taken

explanation.surface: Tidying up the grass courts every so often, against American customs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Regular' takes AN from lawn, and 'ordered' shuffles AN with MANICURE.
explanation.definitionFit: Something un-American goes against the customs or values held to be those of the United States.

clue.text: Something for Laver (not Rosewall) initially suffering with sunburnt head?

definitions.text: Something for Laver (not Rosewall) initially suffering with sunburnt head?

indicators.note: head means just the first letter of sunburnt
suffering means in a bad way, so the letters are rearranged
not signals that a letter is removed from Laver
initially means the first letter of Rosewall is the one removed

explanation.surface: Something Rod Laver, not Ken Rosewall, might need for a burnt scalp.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not' with 'initially' drops R from LAVER, leaving LAVE; 'head' gives S, and 'suffering' shuffles LAVES. Laver and Rosewall are Australian tennis greats.
explanation.definitionFit: A salve is a soothing ointment, the kind rubbed on sunburn.

clue.text: Used lob in this event?

parts.note: the second word of the answer has the letters of these words; the first word says to jumble them

explanation.surface: A tennis lob played in some particular competition.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as an instruction, the answer says the letters of DOUBLES are scrambled, which gives USED LOB.
explanation.definitionFit: Mixed doubles is a tennis event in which each pair is one man and one woman.

clue.text: Look into top player's huge pulsating body

parts.note: to X-ray something is to look inside it
a star is a leading player

explanation.surface: Examining the enormous throbbing physique of the world number one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'body' suggests a sportsman's physique, but it is a celestial body.
explanation.definitionFit: An X-ray star is a stellar object emitting X-rays, often in pulses, a massive celestial body.

clue.text: See 23
Connors' victims, say, drop pretence on air

indicators.note: on air means broadcast, so the word is as heard

parts.note: a guise is a false appearance or pretence

explanation.surface: Jimmy Connors' beaten opponents abandon their act on the radio.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Connors' is not Jimmy Connors the player but con men, whose victims are dupes.
explanation.definitionFit: A fall guy is a dupe or scapegoat, the kind of person a con man exploits.

clue.text: Ivan Lendl ultimately got a hammering here

definitions.text: Ivan Lendl ultimately got a hammering here

indicators.note: got a hammering means was battered about, so the letters of Ivan are rearranged
ultimately means at the end, so the last letter of Lendl

explanation.surface: Ivan Lendl eventually lost heavily at this venue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'got a hammering' shuffles IVAN to ANVI and 'ultimately' adds the L; the whole clue describes the blacksmith's block.
explanation.definitionFit: An anvil is the iron block on which metal is beaten with a hammer.

clue.text: Nadal's furious about cocaine affair

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the letters go round the drug abbreviation
furious means wildly angry, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: C is slang shorthand for cocaine

explanation.surface: Rafael Nadal is enraged by a story about drug-taking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'furious' turns NADALS into SANDAL, which goes 'about' C.
explanation.definitionFit: A scandal is a disgraceful affair causing public outrage.

clue.text: Was Laver a gentleman? Yes, but with a mean streak

indicators.note: with says the letters are contained within the words that follow, a streak running through them

explanation.surface: Asking whether Rod Laver was courteous, and conceding he had a nasty side.
explanation.walkthrough: The run sits in lAVER A GEntleman: Laver has the 'mean streak' in him. 'mean' looks like nasty but is the arithmetic sense.
explanation.definitionFit: An average is the arithmetic mean of a set of numbers.

clue.text: Former champion has heart trouble covering centre of courts

indicators.note: covering means wrapped around the middle letters
trouble means disorder, so the letters are rearranged
centre of means the middle letters of courts

explanation.surface: An ex-champion suffers a heart condition affecting him on court.
explanation.walkthrough: 'trouble' rearranges HASHEART and 'covering' puts UR, the 'centre of' courts, inside. Arthur Ashe won Wimbledon in 1975.
explanation.definitionFit: Arthur Ashe won Wimbledon, the US Open and the Australian Open, a past title holder.

clue.text: Invitation to sporty afternoons in middle of Kenya?

indicators.note: sporty suggests playing about, so the letters are rearranged
middle of means the inner letters of Kenya, without its ends

explanation.surface: An invitation to games on sunny afternoons in central Kenya.
explanation.walkthrough: 'middle of' gives ENY from Kenya, and 'sporty' shuffles AFTERNOONS IN ENY.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a stock casual offer to play a game, so an invitation.

clue.text: No laughs disrupted Evert's closing attack

indicators.note: disrupted means thrown into disorder, so the letters are rearranged
closing means the final letter of Evert's

explanation.surface: Lack of humour broke Chris Evert's final assault.
explanation.walkthrough: 'disrupted' turns NOLAUGHS into ONSLAUGH and 'closing' adds T.
explanation.definitionFit: An onslaught is a fierce or violent attack.

clue.text: Remove judge from early contest

indicators.note: from says the judge is taken away from the contest

parts.note: a joust was a medieval contest between knights

explanation.surface: Get rid of the umpire from an opening-round match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'early' means historical, not first round: a joust was a medieval contest.
explanation.definitionFit: To oust is to drive out or remove from a position.

clue.text: See 22
Rally dimly recalled somewhat blissful time

indicators.note: recalled says the hidden letters are read backwards
somewhat says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Someone vaguely remembers a long rally from a happy period.
explanation.walkthrough: 'somewhat' picks LLYDI from raLLY DImly and 'recalled' reads it backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: An idyll is a period or scene of perfect happiness.

clue.text: Replayed points at end of final scrappy set

indicators.note: at end of means the last letter of final
scrappy means messy and disorganised, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Points were played again at the close of an untidy final set.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Replayed points' fits the tennis surface: in tennis a let is called when a serve clips the net and is played again; 'scrappy' signals the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: In tennis a let is a serve replayed, usually after clipping the net.

clue.text: Smith has dubious hit disallowed — this one?

definitions.text: Smith has dubious hit disallowed — this one?

indicators.note: dubious means questionable, so the letters are shaken up once the other word is taken away

explanation.surface: A player called Smith has a questionable shot ruled out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'disallowed' removes HIT from SMITHHAS, and 'dubious' rearranges what is left; the whole clue describes the shot.
explanation.definitionFit: A smash is a hard overhead shot in tennis, a kind of hit.

clue.text: Fractious McEnroe's last noisy abuse on court

definitions.text: Fractious McEnroe's last noisy abuse on court

indicators.note: fractious means irritable and unruly, so the letters are rearranged
last means the final letter of McEnroe, ignoring the possessive

explanation.surface: John McEnroe, bad-tempered, finally hurls loud insults on court.
explanation.walkthrough: 'last' gives E, and 'Fractious' shuffles it with NOISY ABUSE ON COURT into McEnroe's famous outburst at an umpire.
explanation.definitionFit: McEnroe shouted this at a Wimbledon umpire in 1981, the classic loud tirade on court.
